CausalChain: Fibrotic liver disease -> Increased ECM stiffness -> Activation of integrin β1/FAK in cancer cells & integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK in resident macrophages -> Cancer cell malignant behavior and macrophage polarization to an M2 phenotype -> Secretion of TGF-β, LOXL2 and ECM remodeling enzymes -> Further increase in matrix stiffness -> Reinforcement of tumor-promoting microenvironment -> Activation of compensatory YAP/TAZ signaling
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in fibrotic liver disease, increased ECM stiffness initiates a dual mechanotransduction response. In cancer cells, ECM stiffness activates integrin β1/FAK signaling, enhancing malignant properties, while in liver-resident macrophages, it triggers integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling that polarizes these cells to an immunosuppressive M2 state. The ensuing secretion of TGF-β, LOXL2, and other ECM remodeling enzymes by M2-like macrophages further increases matrix stiffness, thereby creating a self-perpetuating pro-tumorigenic feedback loop. Additionally, high stiffness conditions induce compensatory activation of YAP/TAZ signaling in both cell types, sustaining this pathogenic state. Therefore, we propose that a therapeutic regimen combining inhibitors targeting integrin β1 and β5 pathways, together with YAP/TAZ modulators—and monitored via real-time single-cell transcriptomics and stiffness-sensing technologies—will interrupt this feed-forward loop by repolarizing macrophages and reducing cancer cell malignancy, ultimately mitigating hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that in fibrotic liver disease, increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness initiates a dual mechanotransduction cascade involving both cancer cells and resident macrophages. Specifically, ECM stiffness activates integrin β1/FAK signaling in malignant hepatocytes, driving cancer cell aggressiveness, while concurrently inducing integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in liver-resident macrophages, which polarizes them toward an immunosuppressive, tumor-supportive M2 phenotype. The M2-like macrophages secrete TGF-β, LOXL2, and other ECM remodeling enzymes that further enhance matrix stiffness, thereby reinforcing a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Under conditions of high stiffness, compensatory activation of YAP/TAZ in both cell types sustains this malignant loop. We further posit that a combinatorial therapeutic strategy—targeting both integrin β1 and β5 pathways alongside YAP/TAZ modulators, and guided by real-time single-cell transcriptomic profiling and nanoscale stiffness-sensing technologies—can reprogram these cells, repolarize macrophages to a tumor-suppressive M1 state, and ultimately impede hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis emphasized a macrophage-centric feed-forward loop driven solely by integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling leading to M2 polarization, with compensatory YAP/TAZ activation and secretion of ECM remodeling factors. In the revised hypothesis, we retain these key elements but integrate an additional cancer cell–intrinsic pathway via integrin β1/FAK, reflecting experimental observations that emphasize cancer cell mechanotransduction. Each step of the original causal chain is maintained: fibrotic liver disease leads to increased ECM stiffness, which activates mechanosensitive pathways (now in two distinct cell types), driving secretion of stiffening factors and further matrix remodeling. The novel therapeutic approach explicitly leverages contemporary single-cell transcriptomics and stiffness-sensing technologies to target both pathways, thereby broadening the scope and practical applicability of the original concept.
